displayQuote: If the path before you is clear, you're probably on someone else's

meta.title: Who really said "If the path before you is clear, you're probably on someone else's"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Credited to Joseph Campbell — and the thought really is his, in print. He published it in Pathways to Bliss, p. xxvi. The famous one-liner is a compression.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'If the path before you is clear, you're probably on someone else's'?
meta.ogDescription: Campbell did write this, at greater length: 'Where there's a way or path, it is someone else's path.' Pathways to Bliss, p. xxvi. The one-liner is a paraphrase.

answer.label: Attributed to
answer.sourceLine: Campbell gets the credit everywhere this line appears, and the thought behind it is not merely his in spirit — he published it. In Pathways to Bliss he writes, “You enter the forest at the darkest point, where there is no path. Where there’s a way or path, it is someone else’s path; each human being is a unique phenomenon” (p. xxvi, as his own estate cites it at the Joseph Campbell Foundation ↗), and The Hero’s Journey puts it as “If there is a path it is someone else’s path and you are not on the adventure.” What nobody has produced is the compressed one-liner: those exact words are cited to no book, lecture, interview or letter, and they are absent from Wikiquote’s Campbell entry ↗, while Quote Investigator has never investigated it ↗. It is a paraphrase of a documented original.

source.heading: A compression of what Campbell published

source.excerpt: If the path before you is clear, you’re probably on someone else’s.
trail: Wikiquote turns up nothing. The Joseph Campbell page ↗ carries sourced sections for The Hero with a Thousand Faces, The Power of Myth, Mythology and the Individual, Sukhavati and Pathways to Bliss, plus a Disputed section for lines with no known origin. This sentence appears in none of them.
Quote Investigator has never run it. A site search ↗ returns no article on this quote at all — so there is no specialist finding to defer to here, and no earlier attestation on record.
The quote sites cite nothing. AZQuotes ↗ runs the line under Campbell’s name with no book, speech, interview or date, and Goodreads ↗ does the same — 703 likes, community-added, source field empty.

Found in Campbell’s own books. Look past those three sources and the parent sentence turns up in print, cited by his own estate: the Joseph Campbell Foundation ↗ quotes “Where there’s a way or path, it is someone else’s path” to Pathways to Bliss, p. xxvi, and the same argument runs in The Hero’s Journey as “If there is a path it is someone else’s path and you are not on the adventure.” The circulating line is a tightening of these: documented idea, documented sentence, undocumented wording.
source.excerptNote: There is a fuller original, and it is Campbell’s. Retelling the thirteenth-century Queste del Saint Graal in his own voice, he describes Arthur’s knights deciding it would be a disgrace to ride out as a group: “Each entered the forest at a point that he himself had chosen, where it was darkest and there was no path. If there is a path it is someone else’s path and you are not on the adventure” (The Hero’s Journey). He states the point flatly in Pathways to Bliss: “You enter the forest at the darkest point, where there is no path. Where there’s a way or path, it is someone else’s path; each human being is a unique phenomenon” (p. xxvi). The line quoted online is that thought squeezed into a dozen words — sharper, more portable, and not in Campbell’s hand.

sourceLink.text: Pathways to Bliss, p. xxvi — quoted and cited by the Joseph Campbell Foundation

source.rightsNote: The circulating one-liner is an unattributed paraphrase, so no rights status attaches to it as such. Campbell’s actual sentences are in copyright: Pathways to Bliss was published by New World Library in 2004, The Hero’s Journey by HarperCollins in 1990, and The Power of Myth ↗ by Doubleday in 1988. His literary legacy is administered by the Joseph Campbell Foundation, established in 1991 by his widow Jean Erdman and his longtime editor Robert Walter.

author.name: Joseph Campbell
author.heading: Joseph Campbell
author.metaLine: 1904–1987 · American mythologist & professor of literature, Sarah Lawrence College
author.bio: Joseph Campbell was an American writer on comparative mythology and comparative religion who taught literature at Sarah Lawrence College for decades before becoming, improbably, a popular figure. His The Hero with a Thousand Faces (1949) proposed that the world’s myths share one underlying adventure — the idea later shorthanded as the hero’s journey — and it has been reshaping novels and films ever since. He died in 1987; the Bill Moyers interviews that made him a household name were broadcast and published the following year, and much of the Campbell now quoted online comes from that late, spoken, posthumously edited body of work — part of why so many “Campbell quotes” are so hard to pin to a page.

cite.sourceCitation: Paraphrase. The documented original is Joseph Campbell, Pathways to Bliss: Mythology and Personal Transformation (New World Library, 2004), p. xxvi: "You enter the forest at the darkest point, where there is no path. Where there's a way or path, it is someone else's path; each human being is a unique phenomenon." Campbell states the same point in The Hero's Journey: Joseph Campbell on His Life and Work (HarperCollins, 1990), retelling the knights of the Queste del Saint Graal: "If there is a path it is someone else's path and you are not on the adventure." The popular one-line wording appears in neither and has not been traced to any work by Campbell.
cite.pageCitation: Quotle.info. “Who really said ‘If the path before you is clear, you're probably on someone else's’?” Last verified 24 Aug 2026.

copyAttribution: “If the path before you is clear, you're probably on someone else's.” — attributed to Joseph Campbell (1904–1987), and a compression of something he did publish. Campbell wrote: “You enter the forest at the darkest point, where there is no path. Where there's a way or path, it is someone else's path; each human being is a unique phenomenon” (Pathways to Bliss, New World Library, 2004, p. xxvi), and “If there is a path it is someone else's path and you are not on the adventure” (The Hero's Journey, 1990). The one-line version quoted online is cited to no work of his. Source: Quotle.info

misattribution.heading: What’s actually wrong here
misattribution.intro: This is not a case of the wrong person getting the credit. It is the subtler and far more common problem: a real thinker’s real, published sentence tightened by an unknown hand into a punchier line he is not known to have written, then circulated for years with his name on it and no citation at all.

items.who: No work is cited for this wording
items.why: AZQuotes ↗ and Goodreads ↗ both publish the line as Campbell’s with no book, no lecture, no date — and a citable original does exist, in Pathways to Bliss at p. xxvi. What they are quoting is not that sentence but a shortened rewrite of it, which is why no page number ever travels with it.

Wikiquote’s Campbell page ↗ does not list it — not among the sourced quotations, and not even in the Disputed section it maintains for Campbell lines with no known origin. Quote Investigator has never published on it.

The neighbouring aphorism — go where there is no path and leave a trail — is routinely pinned on Emerson. Quote Investigator traces it instead to Muriel Strode ↗, published in The Open Court in August 1903, and finds the Emerson linkage arose many years after his death. Worth knowing, because the two lines are often quoted side by side and neither belongs to the name on the caption.

misattribution.truthLine: The narrow, defensible statement is this: Joseph Campbell wrote that a path already laid out for you is somebody else’s path, in those words — “Where there’s a way or path, it is someone else’s path”, Pathways to Bliss, p. xxvi ↗ — but the one-line version quoted in his name is a later compression that no work of his contains.

context.heading: Why it sounds so exactly like him
lead: Campbell spent fifty years on one stubborn idea: that the life worth living is the one nobody has already lived for you. So a line about distrusting a clear path doesn’t merely sound like Campbell — it reads like the compressed executive summary of his whole career. That is precisely what makes it slippery. A quote that fits an author perfectly is the hardest kind to doubt, and the easiest kind for someone else to write on his behalf.

What he actually wrote runs longer and reads stranger. Retelling the Grail knights who thought it a disgrace to ride out as a group, Campbell — in his own voice, not an interviewer’s — writes that “each entered the forest at a point that he himself had chosen, where it was darkest and there was no path,” and draws the moral: “If there is a path it is someone else’s path and you are not on the adventure.” In Pathways to Bliss he says it flatly: “Where there’s a way or path, it is someone else’s path; each human being is a unique phenomenon.” It is the same argument, and it is his. It is simply not the same sentence — and nobody has shown who did the squeezing.
detailsBody: Two things make a Campbell attribution unusually hard to test. First, an enormous amount of him exists as talk rather than text — lectures, seminars, broadcast interviews — some later transcribed into books by editors, much of it not. A line could in principle come from a recording nobody has indexed. Second, his estate’s posthumous publishing programme keeps introducing new Campbell “quotes” from compilations, which blurs where any given sentence was first fixed in print.

So the honest verdict is not that Campbell never said this. He said it — at greater length, in books with page numbers. What nobody has shown is where the compressed version came from: Wikiquote does not carry it, Quote Investigator has never run it, and the aggregators reprint it with the citation field empty. That keeps it in the attributed column, not because the thought is doubtful but because the wording is somebody else’s work. Quoting it fairly means citing p. xxvi and letting Campbell’s own sentence do the job.
context.pull: He wrote it longer. Someone else made it quotable.

sourcesVerified.claim: The Joseph Campbell Foundation, Campbell's own estate, quotes "You enter the forest at the darkest point, where there is no path. Where there's a way or path, it is someone else's path; each human being is a unique phenomenon" and cites it to Pathways to Bliss, page xxvi.

Goodreads' quotation page for The Hero's Journey: Joseph Campbell on His Life and Work carries, under Campbell's name, "They thought that it would be a disgrace to go forth as a group. Each entered the forest at a point that he himself had chosen, where it was darkest and there was no path. If there is a path it is someone else's path and you are not on the adventure."
Open Library gives Pathways to Bliss: Mythology and Personal Transformation by Joseph Campbell as first published in 2004 by New World Library.
The Hero's Journey: Joseph Campbell on His Life and Work was originally published by HarperCollins in 1990, with later editions from Element Books (1999) and New World Library (2003).
Goodreads carries the wording "If the path before you is clear, you're probably on someone else's" credited to Joseph Campbell, community-added with 703 likes and no book or source attribution.
AZQuotes shows the identical wording credited to Joseph Campbell and cites no book, speech, interview or date as its source.

Wikiquote's Joseph Campbell page has sourced sections for The Hero with a Thousand Faces (1949), The Power of Myth (1988), Mythology and the Individual (1997), Sukhavati (2002) and Pathways to Bliss (2004), plus a Disputed section; no section contains this wording.
A site search of Quote Investigator for this quote returns no article about it; the results returned are unrelated investigations.

Quote Investigator concludes that the similar 'go where there is no path and leave a trail' saying originated with Muriel Strode, published in The Open Court in August 1903, and that its linkage to Ralph Waldo Emerson occurred many years after his death and is not substantive.
The Internet Archive record for The Power of Myth gives Joseph Campbell (interviewee) with Bill Moyers (interviewer), publisher Doubleday, 1988, 231 pages, an access-restricted lending item.

Wikipedia gives Joseph Campbell's dates as 26 March 1904 to 30 October 1987, describes him as a professor of literature at Sarah Lawrence College specialising in comparative mythology and comparative religion, dates the Moyers interview series broadcast to 1988 (the year following his death), and states the Joseph Campbell Foundation was established in 1991 by Jean Erdman and Robert Walter to manage his literary legacy.
